newsitem.title: BELGIUM: OLOs could get 'bad' data needed to shine again.
newsitem.headline: OLOs could get 'bad' data needed to shine again.

text.p: Belgian government bonds (OLOs) and futures need indications of pick-ups in growth and inflation to pry prices loose from current levels, dealers said on Monday after another session of lacklustre trade.

"The market is looking for direction...it is stuck between a very rosy situation in the U.S. and improving growth in Europe where high unemployment rates are keeping wage inflation down," analyst Conrad Fieremans at Kredietbank said.
He said that while the situation in Europe was favourable yields might rise in coming months on the back of fresh evidence of strength in the buoyant U.S. economy.
Strong economic data are as a rule bad for bonds since growth tends to absorb credit, forcing interest rates up.

For now, however, the mood in U.S. Treasuries was good. Although this week's U.S. data -- June consumer confidence (due on Tuesday) and June durable goods (due on Wednesday) were notoriously volatile, they were not expected to spoil the broth.

Similarly, German CPI data, also due this week, were expected to be benign, not signalling much change from May's west German month-on-month inflation of 0.4 percent and 1.5 percent year-on-year. Belgium's National Bank economic indicator and CPI would also not stir the market, analysts said.

Belgian inflation might rise on the back of seasonally higher vegetable and fresh fruit prices, and import prices boosted by dollar strength, to 0.1 month-on-month and 1.7 percent year-on-year, but the overall picture in Belgium was still benign, analysts said.
Central bank policy in the U.S. -- the FOMC meets next week -- and in Germany -- the Bundesbank council meets on Thursday -- was not expected to be changed.
But, Fieremans warned, weightier U.S. data would be due next week and could point to the strength needed to spark the correction which bond markets were waiting for.
"The combination of steady monetary policy and strong data could paint the picture needed for lower prices," he said. Also, the market was overbought from a chart-technical point of view.

This week it was still too early to buy bonds, he said, a yield of 5.75 percent on the benchmark 10-year OLO BE286= was a level to take profits at, while buyers would not be seen until six percent was reached.

The benchmark yielded 5.81 percent at 1455 GMT, up slightly from Friday's late 5.80 percent. September OLO futures, the new benchmark contract, was up 0.05 basis points at 120.75. June futures expire on June 25.

Fieremans said 10-year German yields could back up to 5.80 or even 5.90 percent in coming months under pressure from the U.S. With an OLO/Bund spread of 5-15 basis points that would put 10-year OLO yields in the vicinity of six percent.
The yield spread was steady at seven basis points at 1515 GMT MEUR.

Higher yields would help investors looking for a end-of- first-half home for their cash balances turn their attention to bonds and away from equities which have been in the limelight for much of the January-June period, analysts said.
